title: R², Adjusted R² and Model Comparison
breadcrumb: Regression → Inference in the linear model → R², adjusted R² and model comparison
engineName: Fit always improves; charge for each parameter and compare only like with like
objectives: Compute adjusted R² from n, k and R², counting k correctly.
State what adding a regressor does to R² and to adjusted R², and why.
Run and read the nested F test, AIC, BIC and Cp for two models.
Recognise a negative adjusted R² and a no-intercept R² that is not comparable.
Decide whether a model comparison is valid before computing it.

traps: Forgetting to subtract from 1 in adjusted R² (0.49 for 0.51).
Counting only the slopes in k, so n − k becomes n − k − 1.
Reading a rise in adjusted R² as significance.
Comparing R² across models with different dependent variables.
Comparing a no-intercept R² with an ordinary one.

sheet: R² = 1 − RSS/TSS; never falls when a regressor is added.
Adjusted R² = 1 − (1 − R²)(n − 1)/(n − k); below R² when k > 1; can be negative.
Negative when R² < (k − 1)/(n − 1): for n = 20, k = 6 the threshold is 0.2632.
n = 50, k = 5, R² = 0.55 gives 0.51 (the Q9 variant).
Adjusted R² rises exactly when |t| of the added coefficient exceeds 1.
Nested F = [(RSS_r − RSS_f)/q]/[RSS_f/(n − k_f)]; example 5.473 against 3.634.
AIC = n ln(RSS/n) + 2k; BIC = n ln(RSS/n) + k ln n; smaller wins; BIC heavier for n ≥ 8.
Cp = RSS_p/σ̂² − (n − 2p); near p for a good subset. Example 10.95 against p = 2.
No-intercept R² uses Σy²; centred it is −2.03 in the example, 0.9227 as reported.
cards: ln n vs 2; BIC heavier for n ≥ 8
tricks: Slopes only is the wrong k; k counts the intercept too.
Check an adjusted R² against R²: it must be a little smaller.
shortcuts: ln 8 = 2.079 is where BIC overtakes AIC.
(k − 1)/(n − 1) is the R² below which adjusted R² is negative.
remember: Compare only models with the same dependent variable.

howto: If short of time, the lesson is scenes 4 (formulas), 5 (the worked comparison) and 9 (the Q9 variant). Skip the extension. It deliberately does not cover multicollinearity (6.5), dummy variables (6.11), cross-validation or stepwise search.

provenance: Anchor: the Q9 variant bank (adjusted R² from n = 50, k = 5, R² = 0.55; adding an irrelevant regressor; adjusted R² can be negative; high R² with insignificant t values). Q9 itself is the F statistic and is taught in topic 6.3. Verified by computing in verify_regression_t1_t4.py: the variant answer 0.51 and its wrong forms (0.49 without the subtraction, 0.4989 with k read as slopes only); the five-student adjusted R² 0.4667 and its wrong forms 0.2 and 0.7; the negative case 0.1, n = 20, k = 6 giving −0.2214 and the threshold 5/19 = 0.2632; the 20-observation comparison: R² 0.8754 and 0.9260, adjusted R² 0.8685 and 0.9121, nested F 1828/334 = 5.473 against 3.634 and its R² form, AIC 126.19 and 119.76, BIC 128.18 and 123.74, Cp 10.95 and 4; ln 8 = 2.079 and ln 7 = 1.946; the no-intercept data giving 0.9227 uncentred, −2.031 centred and 0.9868 with an intercept. scenes.title: Before the lesson — four things it will assume
scenes.objective: Check R², the two degrees-of-freedom counts, nested models and the F statistic.

ask.q: Why is R² alone a poor way to choose between a small model and a larger one?
ask.nudge: What happens to the residual sum of squares when a regressor is added?

body: R² answers one question: what share of the variation in y does the fitted model explain. It cannot answer a different question: is the extra regressor worth keeping. Adding any regressor, even a column of random numbers, leaves R² the same or higher. So a rule that picks the model with the highest R² always picks the biggest model.

Two repairs exist. Adjusted R² divides each sum of squares by its degrees of freedom, so a parameter must pay for itself. Information criteria add a penalty per parameter directly. A third tool, the F test for nested models, asks whether the drop in the residual sum of squares is larger than chance would give.

Part of Q9's bank asks for adjusted R² from n, k and R², and for what adding a regressor does. The working is one line; the usual loss is in the choice between n − k and n − k − 1, and in forgetting to subtract from 1. This lesson fixes the count first, then checks each answer against R² itself.

items.ask: Define R² for a model with an intercept, and give its range.
refresh: R² is the explained share of the total variation. For the five-student data R² = 3.6/6 = 0.6. With an intercept it cannot be negative and cannot exceed 1.
It is also the squared correlation between y and the fitted values. It does not say whether the model is correct, only how closely it fits.

items.ask: What are the degrees of freedom of RSS and of TSS?
refresh: From topic 6.1 the residuals live in a space of dimension tr(M) = n − k, where k counts every coefficient including the intercept. TSS has n − 1 because the deviations from the mean add to zero.
In Q9's variant the quantity k = 5 counts all five parameters, so n − k = 45 when n = 50. Reading k as the number of slopes only would give 44, which is a different answer.

items.ask: What does it mean for two models to be nested?
items.recall: The smaller model is the larger one with some coefficients set to zero.
refresh: Model B is nested in model A if B is A with a set of restrictions, usually some coefficients fixed at zero. Then A can fit everything B can, so RSS_A ≤ RSS_B.
Models using different regressors, none containing the other, are non-nested. The F test below does not apply to them.

items.ask: State the F statistic for H₀: all slopes zero in terms of R².
refresh: From topic 6.3. It divides the explained share by its degrees of freedom and the unexplained share by its own. The numerator degrees of freedom are the number of slopes.
The nested version replaces R² by the increase in R² and k − 1 by the number of restrictions q.

scenes.title: Fit always improves; the question is whether it improves enough
scenes.objective: Explain why R² cannot choose a model, and what adjusted R² charges.
body: Adding a regressor gives the least-squares fit one more direction to use. At worst it ignores it, so the residual sum of squares cannot rise, and R² cannot fall. That is a fact about geometry, not about whether the new variable is relevant.

A fair comparison has to charge for the extra direction. Adjusted R² does so by replacing each sum of squares with its average per degree of freedom: 1 − [RSS/(n − k)] / [TSS/(n − 1)]. Adding a regressor lowers n − k, which raises the first average unless RSS falls enough to compensate. The exact break-even is simple: adjusted R² rises precisely when the new coefficient's t statistic exceeds 1 in absolute value.
That break-even is lenient. A t of 1.1 is nowhere near significant, yet adjusted R² rises. Adjusted R² is a mild penalty. The F test, AIC and BIC apply stronger ones.

scenario.teaser: Two models for the same twenty observations, one with two extra regressors.
scenario.title: Is the larger model worth it?
body: An analyst has 20 observations with total variation TSS = 72214. A model with two parameters, an intercept and one regressor, leaves a residual sum of squares of 9000, so R² = 0.875. A larger model with four parameters leaves RSS = 5344, so R² = 0.926.

The larger model has the higher R², by construction. Adjusted R² gives 0.9121 against 0.8685, so the larger model still wins after the charge for two extra parameters. The nested F test asks whether the drop of 3656 in RSS, spread over the two added coefficients, is large compared with the residual average 5344/16 = 334: F = 1828/334 = 5.47, which exceeds the 5% point of F(2, 16), 3.634.

AIC agrees (119.76 against 126.19) and so does BIC (123.74 against 128.18). When four criteria point the same way the choice is easy. The interesting cases are those where they disagree, and the lesson shows why.
scenario.q: Which of R², adjusted R² and the nested F test could not have favoured the smaller model if the larger model's RSS were lower?
scenario.answer: R². Adding regressors never raises RSS, so R² always favours the larger model. Adjusted R² and F can favour the smaller model if the drop in RSS is too small.

ask.q: Does a rise in adjusted R² after adding a regressor mean that regressor is significant?
ask.nudge: What t statistic is the break-even?

scenes.title: How large must R² be to count?
scenes.objective: See that the evidence R² gives depends on n, and find the threshold for one regressor at n = 20.

viz.caption: Set n = 20. With one regressor, R² = r², and the 5% two-sided critical |r| is about 0.444, so R² must exceed 0.197.

body: With a single regressor R² is the square of the correlation r. The picture shows how r behaves when the true correlation is zero. At n = 20 the 5% two-sided critical value is |r| = 0.444, so R² has to exceed 0.197 before it is evidence of anything.
Slide n to 5 and the threshold becomes 0.771. Slide to 60 and it falls below 0.07. The same R² means different things in different sample sizes.
This is why R² should be read with n and k beside it, and why adjusted R² and the F test bring them in.

ask.q: Would an R² of 0.15 be significant at n = 20 with one regressor?

scenes.title: R², adjusted R², F for nested models, AIC, BIC and Cp
scenes.objective: State each criterion and what it penalises.

blocks.body: R̄² < R² whenever k > 1, and R̄² can be negative. It is negative when R² < (k − 1)/(n − 1). It never exceeds 1. It equals 1 − s²/s_y², where s² is the residual variance estimate and s_y² the sample variance of y.

F = [(RSS_r − RSS_f)/q] / [RSS_f/(n − k_f)]
  = [(R²_f − R²_r)/q] / [(1 − R²_f)/(n − k_f)]
on (q, n − k_f) degrees of freedom.

AIC = n ln(RSS/n) + 2k
BIC = n ln(RSS/n) + k ln n
Smaller is better. BIC's penalty per parameter ln n exceeds AIC's 2 once n ≥ 8.

Cp = RSS_p/σ̂² − (n − 2p),   σ̂² = RSS of the full model/(n − k_full)
For a model with little bias, Cp is close to its parameter count p.

flow.title: Choosing how to compare models
flow.alt: A top-to-bottom flow. First check the dependent variable is the same. If the models are nested use the F test. If not, use AIC or BIC. Adjusted R squared is a quick screen.

nodes.label: Yes: F test on the added coefficients
No: compare AIC or BIC (lower wins)
Different y: no valid comparison on R² or RSS

flow.note: R² and RSS from regressions with different dependent variables (for example y and ln y) are not comparable.

scenes.title: Comparing two models on twenty observations, every criterion
scenes.objective: Compute R², adjusted R², nested F, AIC, BIC and Cp for the models in the first scenario.

ask.q: Do all the criteria prefer the larger model?

scenes.problem: n = 20, TSS = 72214. Model R (k = 2): RSS = 9000. Model F (k = 4): RSS = 5344. Compare them.

steps.why: The larger model's R² is higher, as it must be.
The factor (n − 1)/(n − k) is 19/18 for the small model and 19/16 for the large one. The larger model survives the charge.

steps.say: Nested F for the two added coefficients (q = 2).
steps.why: 5.473 > 3.634, so reject the restrictions. The same F in R² form: [(0.9260 − 0.8754)/2]/[0.0740/16].
Smaller is better, so both prefer F. The difference is 6.43 for AIC and 4.43 for BIC.
A Cp far above p signals that the small model is biased, which agrees with the F test. For the full model Cp = 4 exactly.

scenes.after: All six measures agree here. When the answer is clear every method finds it; the value of knowing them is for the unclear cases.

items.q: Write adjusted R² in terms of R², n and k.
Does adding a regressor lower R²?
items.a: Never. It stays the same or rises.

items.q: When does adjusted R² rise on adding a regressor?
items.a: Exactly when the new coefficient's |t| exceeds 1.

items.q: Which is larger, BIC's penalty per parameter or AIC's, for n = 20?

scenes.title: Your turn — a negative adjusted R²
scenes.objective: Compute adjusted R² for a poorly fitting model with many parameters.
scenes.problem: n = 20, k = 6 parameters and R² = 0.10. Find the adjusted R².

steps.why: 0.9 is the share the model leaves unexplained.

blank.prompt: What is the adjusted R², to two decimals?

steps.why: 0.2632. R² = 0.10 is below it, so the adjusted value must be negative, as found.

scenes.after: A negative adjusted R² is a signal, not an error: the model fits worse than a constant once its parameters are charged.

scenes.title: Why adjusted R² rises exactly when |t| > 1, and the no-intercept trap
scenes.objective: Derive the break-even for adjusted R² and explain why R² from a model with no intercept cannot be compared.

blocks.body: R̄² = 1 − s²/s_y², with s_y² = TSS/(n − 1) unchanged when a regressor is added. So R̄² rises exactly when s² = RSS/(n − k) falls.

Let m = n − k before the addition. Adding one regressor with t statistic t gives RSS_old = RSS_new·(1 + t²/(m − 1)). Then s²_new < s²_old when RSS_new/(m − 1) < RSS_new(1 + t²/(m − 1))/m. Multiply out by m(m − 1)/RSS_new: m < m − 1 + t², which is t² > 1.

Start with n = 20, k = 3, R² = 0.5, so R̄² = 0.4412. Add a regressor with t = 0.8: R² rises to 0.5192 but R̄² falls to 0.4291. With |t| = 1 exactly R̄² is unchanged. A check on 4000 random data sets confirmed the rule every time, and that R² never fell.

When the model has no intercept the software reports an uncentred R² = 1 − RSS/Σy². For y = 10, 12, 13, 15, 16 on x = 1..5 the no-intercept fit gives 0.9227 and the model with an intercept gives 0.9868. Measured against the centred total, the no-intercept fit gives −2.03. The two R² values are on different scales and must not be compared.
R² and RSS from a regression of ln y cannot be compared with those of a regression of y. Their totals measure different things. AIC, after adding the Jacobian term, can compare them; plain R² cannot.

ask.q: Why is |t| > 1 a weak test for keeping a regressor?
ask.nudge: Compare with the usual critical value near 2.

scenes.title: On your own — adjusted R² from n, k and R²
scenes.objective: Compute adjusted R² for the Q9 variant and check it.
scenes.problem: With n = 50, k = 5 and R² = 0.55, find the adjusted R².
hints: Direction: decide what k counts. Here k = 5 is the number of parameters, so n − k = 45.
Next step: compute 0.45 × 49/45 first, then subtract from 1.
scenes.check: The answer must lie below R² = 0.55 and close to it, since n is large relative to k. The value 0.49 is the unexplained share and 0.45 is 1 − R².

scenario.teaser: A regression through the origin reports an R² that looks better than the same model with an intercept.
scenario.title: The R² that looks too good
body: An analyst fits y on x for five points, x = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and y = 10, 12, 13, 15, 16, once with an intercept and once forcing the line through the origin. The software reports R² = 0.9868 for the first and R² = 0.9227 for the second.

The second figure uses a different denominator. With no intercept the software compares RSS with Σy², the total about zero, rather than with the total about the mean. That denominator is much larger, because the y values are far from zero, which flatters the fit.

Measure the no-intercept fit against the usual centred total and R² becomes −2.03. A line forced through the origin fits these data far worse than a horizontal line at the mean. The reported 0.9227 hid that.
scenario.q: Can the R² of a no-intercept model be compared with the R² of a model with an intercept?
scenario.answer: No. They use different totals. On a common, centred footing the no-intercept fit is −2.03 against 0.9868.

solution.why: k counts every parameter, including the intercept.
The inflation 49/45 raises the unexplained share from 0.45 to 0.49.
If k = 5 had counted only the slopes the divisor would be 44 and the answer 0.4989, which rounds to 0.50. Read the definition of k.

scenes.title: Six statements
scenes.objective: Separate true properties of the criteria from tempting false ones.
scenes.intro: Decide true or false on all six before revealing any.

items.claim: Adding an irrelevant regressor can lower R².
items.why: R² stays the same or rises. Least squares can always set the new coefficient to zero.
It is negative when R² < (k − 1)/(n − 1). For R² = 0.10, n = 20, k = 6 it is −0.2214.

items.claim: A rise in adjusted R² after adding a regressor shows that its coefficient is significant at 5%.
items.why: The break-even is |t| > 1. Significance at 5% needs |t| above about 2.

items.claim: The nested F test can compare a model in x with a model in a different set of regressors that does not contain it.
items.why: It needs nested models, the smaller one obtained from the larger by restrictions.

items.claim: BIC penalises an extra parameter more heavily than AIC once n ≥ 8.
items.why: The BIC penalty per parameter is ln n, which exceeds 2 from n = 8 (ln 8 = 2.079).

items.claim: R² can be used to compare a regression of y with a regression of ln y.
items.why: The dependent variables differ, so the totals differ. The R² values are not on a common footing.

scenes.title: Transfer — what a weak regressor does
scenes.objective: Predict the effect of adding a regressor with a small t statistic.
scenes.problem: A model with n = 20, k = 3 and R² = 0.5 gains a fourth parameter whose t statistic is 0.8. Find the new R² and adjusted R², and say what happened.
hints: Direction: first find the old adjusted R² from n, k and R².
Method: RSS_old/RSS_new = 1 + t²/(m − 1), where m = n − k_old = 17.
Next step: the new unexplained share is 0.5 divided by that ratio; then apply the adjustment with k = 4.
scenes.answer: R² rises from 0.5 to 0.5192; adjusted R² falls from 0.4412 to 0.4291, because |t| = 0.8 < 1.
scenes.check: R² must rise or stay put, and adjusted R² must fall because |t| < 1.

solution.why: The new regressor trims RSS by under 4%.
The fit gained little and the extra parameter was charged more than it earned.

scenes.title: Where this sits in the syllabus
scenes.objective: Place model comparison against the topics around it.

blocks.body: The sums of squares and the F statistic are from topic 6.3, and the counts n − k and n − 1 from topic 6.1.
Topic 6.5 explains why a high R² can sit beside insignificant t statistics: near multicollinearity. Topic 6.11 uses nested F tests to compare models with and without dummy variables.
Cross-validation, likelihood-ratio tests beyond the Gaussian case, and stepwise search are not covered. AIC and BIC appear here as formulas with Gaussian errors only.

scenes.title: What you should now be able to do
scenes.objective: Check the lesson against its objectives.
body: Compute adjusted R² from n, k and R², with k counting every parameter.
State that R² never falls when a regressor is added and that adjusted R² rises exactly when |t| > 1.
Run the nested F test in RSS and R² forms.
Compare AIC, BIC and Cp values and know which direction wins.

scenes.title: Extension — the identity behind the break-even

blocks.body: Dropping one regressor from the larger model is a single restriction. The F statistic is (RSS_old − RSS_new)/(RSS_new/(m − 1)), where m − 1 = n − k_new.
For one restriction the partial F equals the square of the t statistic of the dropped coefficient, as shown in topic 6.3. So RSS_old − RSS_new = t²·RSS_new/(m − 1).
RSS_old = RSS_new(1 + t²/(m − 1)). This is the identity used in the break-even and in the transfer example.
